figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Soft-MTP’s illustration, pseudocode, and loss performance compared to MTP. Blue line is the one-line code change. We refer readers to Algorithm 1 for the full code implementation of Soft-MTP, including the MTP loss weighting.
figures.headline: Soft-MTP changes one line of standard MTP code and routes gradients through a straight-through path.
citing_sentences: This trick enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), which removes the residual and sends only the useful KL self-distillation gradient through the MTP heads and the shared model trunk, with a one-line code change (see Figure 1).
Figure 1 illustrates the straight-through gradient routing and the one-line code change needed to operationalize the KL gradient–recovery.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Illustration of position-aligned NTP distributions.
figures.headline: For K equals 2, each MTP prediction is paired with the NTP distribution from the later position that predicts the same token.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 provides a visualization of the position-aligned NTP distributions for an MTP model with $K=2$.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The residual has substantially lower SNR than the KL gradient but dominates the MTP gradient signal. (a-b) Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of each gradient component with respect to the shared trunk and MTP head parameters, across scales. (c) Share of the MTP gradient in the shared trunk carried by each component, averaged over training steps; the residual carries $\sim$80% at every scale.
figures.headline: The residual has lower signal-to-noise ratio than the KL component yet supplies about 80% of the MTP gradient reaching the trunk.
citing_sentences: Figures 3(a) and 3(b) compare the SNR of the two gradient components w.r.t. the shared trunk and MTP head parameters across model scales.
Yet despite its low SNR, the residual accounts for $\sim$80% of the MTP gradient reaching the shared trunk (see Figure 3(c)).

Thus, although the standard MTP contains the high SNR KL signal implicitly, the residual obscures it under high-variance updates, which is why the overall hard-MTP gradient has lower SNR (see Figure 3(b)).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: The residual worsens NTP and MTP loss especially as scale increases. (a) Change in NTP loss $\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\text{NTP}}$ from a unit step of the trunk hidden state representation along each gradient component across model scales. (b-c) NTP and MTP loss of standard MTP and Soft-MTP throughout training across scales.
figures.headline: A step along the residual raises NTP loss, and removing the residual lowers NTP loss more as scale grows.
citing_sentences: In Figure 4(a), we take a unit step on the shared trunk’s hidden state along each component’s gradient (backpropagated from the MTP heads) and re-evaluate the NTP loss through the frozen output head.
We empirically corroborate this residual interference in Figure 4(b): removing the residual with Soft-MTP lowers the NTP loss, especially as scale increases.
Furthermore, from 689M parameters onward, Soft-MTP also reaches a lower MTP loss than standard MTP (see Figure 4(c)).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Effect of MTP weight and prediction horizon for 332M models trained on 7.3B tokens. Every axis is lower-better. (a-b) Varying MTP weight $\lambda_{\text{MTP}}\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}$ at fixed horizon $K=3$. Soft-MTP dominates the Pareto frontier for both plots. (c-d) Varying horizon $K\in\{3,4,5,6,7,8\}$ at fixed $\lambda_{\text{MTP}}=1.0$. Soft-MTP leads on both axes at every $K$ shown.
figures.headline: At 332M, Soft-MTP reaches lower NTP and MTP loss than standard MTP at every MTP weight and every horizon tested.
citing_sentences: Lowering $\lambda_{\text{MTP}}$ trades MTP loss for NTP performance, but Figure 5(a) shows that at every weight, Soft-MTP reaches lower NTP and MTP loss than standard MTP, so it Pareto-dominates standard MTP.
The same holds for NTP loss against KL to the NTP verifier (see Figure 5(b)).

Next, sweeping over MTP horizons while keeping $\lambda_{\text{MTP}}$ fixed at 1.0, Soft-MTP also achieves lower NTP and MTP loss than standard MTP at every horizon from $K=3$ to $K=8$ (see Figures 5(c) and 5(d)).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Effective rank of the logit map $W_{\gamma}$. Soft-MTP stays closest to the next-token readout.
figures.headline: Standard MTP cuts the logit map's effective rank to 131 from an NTP baseline of 496; Soft-MTP stays at 437.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 shows the consequence for the readout’s geometry, measured by the effective rank (Roy and Vetterli, 2007) of the logit map $W_{\gamma}$, the unembedding combined with the final RMSNorm gain $\gamma$ (we combine the two because the logits depend only on their product).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Validation NTP and MTP losses of standard MTP and Soft-MTP with Meta-style MTP heads at 332M.
figures.headline: With Meta-style MTP heads at 332M, Soft-MTP reaches lower NTP and MTP validation loss than standard MTP at the end of training.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 shows that Soft-MTP attains lower NTP and MTP loss than standard MTP at the end of training.

abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model’s own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient–recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.

sections.body: The paper argues that the standard MTP cross-entropy gradient mixes a useful KL self-distillation term with a residual. The residual has a low signal-to-noise ratio and interferes with both NTP and MTP learning, more so at larger scale. The authors introduce the KL gradient–recovery trick, which recovers the KL gradient from two cross-entropy gradients through straight-through routing, with no vocabulary-sized logit matrices. Soft-MTP applies it as a one-line code change. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, the paper reports lower NTP perplexity, faster self-speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy than standard MTP.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Standard MTP training contains a residual gradient that interferes with learning, which Soft-MTP removes.

sections.body: This section places the work among three lines of research. MTP began with blockwise parallel decoding and ProphetNet, was shown to help code with parallel heads, and was brought to frontier pre-training by DeepSeek-V3's sequential modules. MTP heads also serve as speculative drafters, and recent work trains drafters to match the verifier more closely. Prior self-distillation methods for MTP compute the KL explicitly, approximate it with top-k logits or argmax predictions, or cache the teacher's contribution while freezing the output head. The authors state that Soft-MTP instead recovers the KL gradient exactly from existing cross-entropy gradients, adding no measurable overhead.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior self-distillation for MTP computes the KL explicitly or approximates it, while Soft-MTP recovers it from existing cross-entropy gradients.

sections.body: The section sets notation. Tokens are one-hot vectors over a vocabulary of size V. A trunk with parameters theta produces a hidden state, and a linear output head W maps it through a softmax to a next-token distribution. The NTP loss is the summed cross-entropy against the data. MTP adds K heads that share the same output head and each predict a token further ahead. The overall loss adds the averaged MTP cross-entropy, weighted by a scalar coefficient, to the NTP loss. Implementations average each loss over its own number of targets, which the paper handles later in Section B.5.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Defines the next-token and multi-token cross-entropy losses for a shared linear output head.

sections.body: The section decomposes the hard MTP gradient at the MTP hidden state. For the k-th head, the hard gradient is W transpose times the difference between the MTP prediction and the one-hot target. It splits exactly into $g_{KL}$, the gradient of a KL divergence from a stop-gradient aligned NTP distribution to the MTP distribution, and $g_{res}$, the NTP cross-entropy gradient against the data. Written as $g_{hard} = g_{KL} + g_{res}$, the split holds exactly for each batch and for both parallel and sequential MTP heads. The residual is the only part that depends on the sampled target token.
sections.heading: Decomposing the MTP Gradient
sections.headline: The MTP cross-entropy gradient splits exactly into a KL self-distillation term and a residual term.

sections.body: This section describes Soft-MTP. The authors add a term to the NTP hidden states that is numerically zero but carries a stop-gradient, so the NTP loss keeps its usual gradient while the MTP hidden states receive $-g_{res}$ from it. Summed with the ordinary MTP gradient, the MTP heads and shared trunk get only $g_{KL}$, and no logit matrices are built. The output head still receives cross-entropy gradients, which Table 1 contrasts with KL-MTP. The section also gives a bias–variance view: the residual's variance comes from sampling one-hot targets, and removing it biases the update toward the NTP distribution rather than the data. The authors call this trade increasingly favorable as scale grows.
sections.heading: Soft Multi-Token Prediction
sections.headline: Soft-MTP sends the KL gradient through MTP heads and trunk by routing a negated residual, avoiding vocabulary-sized logits.

sections.body: Models are LLaMA-style, from 167M to 1.2B parameters, with three DeepSeek-style MTP heads and an MTP loss weight of 1.0. Training uses FineWeb-Edu for 60,000 steps, about 31.5B tokens, with the Muon optimizer. The residual has roughly 4× lower signal-to-noise ratio than the KL component, widening from 4.1× at 167M to 4.6× at 1.2B, and it carries ~80% of the MTP gradient reaching the shared trunk. Soft-MTP gives lower NTP loss, lower MTP loss from 689M parameters onward, and better self-speculative decoding and downstream accuracy than standard MTP. At 1.2B it matches or exceeds direct KL minimization on most metrics.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP across 167M to 1.2B parameters on speculative decoding and downstream accuracy.

sections.body: This section argues that the trick is compatible with frontier parallelism. It needs the NTP and MTP hidden states on the same device and a backward path, so it adds no communication for parameter, optimizer or expert sharding. Pipeline parallelism works if the MTP modules sit on the output head's stage, which DeepSeek-V3 already does. Only sequence sharding adds communication: a backward exchange of at most K hidden-state gradients at each shard boundary, independent of sequence length. An explicit KL needs vocabulary-sized distributions for both models, which fused cross-entropy kernels cannot compute without materializing logits. The authors say MTP's longevity in pre-training is uncertain, since DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash dropped MTP.
sections.heading: Discussion: Practical Relevance at Frontier Scale
sections.headline: The trick needs extra communication only under sequence sharding and avoids vocabulary-sized KL tensors.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the decomposition: standard MTP cross-entropy splits into a KL self-distillation term and a residual that is the next-token cross-entropy gradient against the data. The residual carries most of the MTP gradient yet has low signal-to-noise, works against NTP learning, and grows noisier with scale. The KL gradient–recovery trick removes it and recovers the KL term exactly from gradients that standard MTP already computes. The resulting Soft-MTP adds no parameters and stays compatible with fused kernels. The authors report gains in NTP and MTP loss, self-speculative decoding, zero-shot accuracy, and math and code reasoning after fine-tuning, all at no extra cost.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Soft-MTP is a one-line change to MTP that adds no parameters and improves NTP loss, speculative decoding and reasoning.

sections.body: The acknowledgements state that most experiments were funded by Jayden and run on eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs rented from Vast.ai. The work was inspired by an attempt to amortize the computational cost of the KL objective in NextLat. The authors thank several named colleagues for discussions and support. Jayden also thanks one colleague for input on figure design and another for support that helped the project finish.

sections.body: Appendix A is the full Soft-MTP PyTorch implementation. Appendix B derives the hard MTP gradient, the KL self-distillation gradient, the parameter-level split, and the gradient recovery trick, including its forward and backward passes and the output head. Appendix D lists training hyperparameters: Muon with momentum 0.95 and AdamW for embeddings, output head and norms, weight decay 0.1, and gradient norm clipping at 1.0. Appendix E defines the signal-to-noise and gradient-share estimators, which use 256 minibatches of 4 sequences. The final figure shows Meta-style validation losses at 332M.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the Soft-MTP PyTorch implementation, gradient derivations, hyperparameters, and signal-to-noise and gradient-share diagnostics.
